awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: 3D Printed Electrodes for High Performance Microbatteries
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will be the development of high energy dense, rechargeable lithium (Li)-ion microbatteries, with a significantly increased energy density per unit area. Such batteries will transform next-generation Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, and wearable devices, such as earbuds, watches and medical sensors. Current microbattery technologies show a critical limitation with regard to the energy, power and life cycle requirements of device makers. This innovation leverages three-dimensional (3D) printed microscale cathode electrodes, while also employing wafer-level processing to achieve superior manufacturing uniformity. The project will impact a Total Available Market (TAM) of $10 billion across the IoT and wearable devices markets. The technology will enable high density batteries that extend the usage of healthcare devices, while opening newer applications that require added computation and power. The project will lead to a robust, reliable, scalable, and commercially viable Li-ion microbattery platform that enables the next generation of microelectronic devices.

The intellectual merit of this project includes utilization of rapid 3D printing to manufacture microlattice cathodes and semiconductor wafer-level manufacturing processes to build microbatteries at scale. The microlattice cathode will have thicknesses of >450 micrometers compared to the current 60-80 micrometers, increasing energy storing material from under 20% to greater than 60% of the battery volume and thus increasing energy storage. The wafer manufacturing process will decrease cost and increase yield to over 95%. The technical challenges to be solved include the printability of conventional and next-generation battery materials and understanding the electrochemical performance of the 3D printed structures and how the structures interact in the semiconductor manufacturing process. Specifically, scientific insights will be gained into the manufacturing process, such as understanding fluid dynamics for the printing process to rapidly build 3D microscale structures. Research objectives include demonstrating the 3D printability of lithium iron phosphate and lithium cobalt oxide cathodes, fabricating hermetically sealed microbattery cells, and proving the repeatability of the cell design and the semiconductor manufacturing process. The anticipated technical results will create a fundamental understanding of 3D printed electrodes and their integration with semiconductor processes, establishing a platform technology for next-generation energy storage solutions that overcome traditional microbattery limitations.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report for the General Public

NSF Award #2451439  |  Power 3D, Inc.  |  "3D Printed Electrodes for High Performance Microbatteries"

Principal Investigator: Chunshan Hu

(a) Project Outcomes

Many of today’s smallest electronic devices, such as hearing aids, medical implants, health-tracking wearables, and compact defense equipment, are limited less by their electronics than by the batteries that power them. Standard battery manufacturing works well for producing flat, rectangular cells in a narrow range of sizes, but it struggles to make batteries that are unusually small, unusually shaped, or packed with as much energy as possible into a tight space. Power 3D set out to address this problem using a specialized 3D printing technique that builds micro-architected battery electrodes layer by layer, allowing more active material to be packed into a given footprint than conventional manufacturing allows.

During this Phase I project, Power 3D demonstrated that aerosol jet printing can create battery electrodes that are both extremely fine-featured and much thicker than conventional electrodes, allowing more energy-storing material to fit into compact device spaces. The printed electrodes achieved commercial-level material performance while enabling battery layouts that can use internal device volume more efficiently than standard micro-batteries. Power 3D also built and tested rechargeable prototype cells, showing that the printed electrodes can function in real battery formats rather than only as laboratory structures. The team further demonstrated that the printing platform can be extended to multiple battery materials, creating a path toward micro-batteries that can outperform current options by combining higher energy density, custom shapes, and application-specific battery design.

A key outcome of this project was a redesign of the battery’s outer casing. Early on, the team used a rigid, computer-chip-style casing, but direct conversations with dozens of prospective customers, mostly makers of wearable devices, showed that the market needs batteries that can be made in unusual, custom shapes, such as thin rectangles, curved forms, or even rings. In response, Power 3D redesigned the casing around a formed-metal approach better suited to custom shapes and lower-cost manufacturing. The project also produced a detailed cost model showing a credible path toward selling cells for less than one dollar each at large production volumes, an important milestone for eventual commercial viability. Outside experts from the University of Pittsburgh, Carnegie Mellon University, and Penn State contributed cleanroom-processing expertise during the project’s early manufacturing evaluations.

(b) Products

This award did not result in any peer-reviewed publications. The primary products of the project are internal engineering data sets, process specifications, and a manufacturing cost model, which Power 3D is using to support a Phase II SBIR proposal for continued development.

(c) Other Information of Public Interest

Power 3D intends to submit a Phase II proposal to the National Science Foundation to continue developing this technology, with a focus on building a small-scale pilot manufacturing line and delivering prototype batteries to real-world customers in the wearable device, medical device, and defense sectors. The company does not have any publications currently planned from this Phase I work, but expects that ongoing development may result in future public disclosures as the technology matures.
